newsitem.title: UK: BUSINESSMAN DENIES HE TRIED TO FIX SOCCER MATCHES.
newsitem.headline: BUSINESSMAN DENIES HE TRIED TO FIX SOCCER MATCHES.

text.p: A Malaysian businessman accused of rigging top English soccer matches said on Wednesday he would never have dared to ask his co-defendants to fix games, he merely asked them to forecast results.

"Imagine if I suggested to (Bruce) Grobbelaar that he fix matches...probably I would be flying from the window of his penthouse," Heng Suan Lim told the court. The prosecution accuses Lim, 31, of receiving around 500,000 pounds ($800,000) from various Asian sources which he then used to pay off members of a match-fixing ring which was working for a Far Eastern betting syndicate.
Lim stands accused with former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, former Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers and former Aston Villa striker John Fashanu. All four deny the charges.
Lim says he merely enlisted the players to help him forecast the outcome of matches for a wealthy Indonesian gambler called Johannes Josef.
Prosecutor David Calvert Smith asked Lim why his frequent telephone conversations with Grobbelaar had halted in early 1994 after the Zimbabwean goalkeeper was dropped from Liverpool's first team.
The calls resumed later the same year after Grobbelaar joined another top-flight team, Southampton.
"There was no contact because Grobbelaar was not playing so there was no opportunity to fix matches," Calvert Smith suggested to Lim.
"He was perfectly capable of predicting how teams were going to play even if he was not playing himself," he added.
Lim denied the accusation, aaying the two men had lost touch because Grobbelaar had been depressed about leaving Liverpool.

He told Calvert Smith it was mere coincidence that two of the players to whom he paid thousands of pounds were goslkeepers. Lim earlier told the court that Josef, a cocoa commodity trader, was merely a kindly father figure.
"Win or lose, he will not moan or show any dissatisfaction -- he bets as a hobby," said Lim.

"Mr Josef does not bet with any syndicate but with friends and associates on a friendly basis. It's very hurtful to suggest I am a representative of this betting syndicate," the otherwise phlegmatic Lim said in an impassioned plea to the jury.

Calvert Smith detailed how the well-dressed Lim had embarked on a string of failed business ventures and indulged his passion for casinos since coming to Britain in 1988. Lim said on Tuesday he had lost 175,000 pounds ($280,000) in casinos.
But his only apparent income came in regular contributions from Josef, whom Lim described as a close friend of his mother.
Lim says he also received money from his mother, an assistant manageress in a Kuala Lumpur night club.
Armed with copies of Lim's bank statements, Calvert Smith pointed to large, specific sums of money paid into Lim's bank which were withdrawn in cash shortly afterwards.
At the same time, Lim was making regular phone calls to Josef, Fashanu, Grobbelaar and Segers, especially on the days of big soccer matches.
Lim has agreed he paid Grobbelaar and Segers for helping him with the match forecasts he provided for Josef, although he said the players would not offer predictions for their own team.
